div.head: Significance
div.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a devastating disease with limited treatment options. We find that EdU in combination with the currently used anticancer drug TMZ produces highly significant survival benefits and synergistic effects in preclinical GBM models. This striking effect presumably results from simultaneously engaging distinct DNA repair pathways and offers a potential tool against this disease.

Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive malignant primary brain tumor in adults, with incidence peaking in later life. It is commonly treated with surgery followed by administration of ionizing radiation and the DNA-alkylating agent temozolomide (TMZ). Even though this regimen confers some progression-free survival, there is essentially no cure with the median survival with the standard of care being about 12 mo. Currently, several alternative approaches are being developed to improve upon this outcome. We have already shown EdU alone effectively treats GBM, and we now study the efficacy of TMZ+EdU combination therapy. TMZ+EdU significantly improves antitumor efficacy compared to either single-agent therapy against GBM cell lines in vitro, against three different orthotopic GBM xenograft models, and against passage-zero GBM patient tumor tissues engrafted within an organotypic brain slice culture-based platform. Together, our results suggest that EdU could be effective alongside standard-of-care TMZ in patients with GBM. glioblastoma (GBM) | temozolomide (TMZ) | 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) | chemotherapy | anticancer drugs

Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most treatment-resistant human cancers, with progression and recurrence as defining features (1 -4). Currently, the standard of care for GBM consists of surgery followed by ionizing radiation and temozolomide (TMZ) drug therapy (5 -7). During TMZ treatment, eventually MGMT (methylguanine methyl transferase) promoter hypermethylation causes silencing of MGMT which plays an essential role in TMZ-initiated death of malignant tumor cells. However, after an initial positive response to multimodal therapy, ~80% of GBM patients experience recurrence at or near the original tumor site (8 -11), often accompanied by new genetic alterations acquired under treatment pressure (12 , 13). At this stage, therapeutic options are limited, and even with standard of care, median survival remains around 12 mo (4 , 11 , 14 ). Recently, a number of new drugs/intervention methods have been developed to improve the management of GBM (15). Among these, 5-ethynyl-2-deoxyuridine (EdU), conceptually, appears to be unique in terms of being immune to resistance development due to its high similarity to thymidine (see Fig. 1 for the chemical structures of TMZ and EdU).

EdU is commonly used to study DNA replication via "click chemistry" (16 -19 ). Fortuitously, we found that EdU incorporated into the human genome is recognized as "damage" and removed from the genome by excision repair in the form of 26 to 27 nt-long oligomers, leading to a futile cycle of incorporation into DNA and its removal (20). is realization, combined with previous reports on toxicity of EdU in tissue culture as well as its established property of crossing the blood-brain barrier suggested EdU might be effective against brain cancer (21 , 22). Previously, we showed that EdU is effective against GBM cell lines in vitro, orthotopic in vivo mouse models of GBM established with intracranial engrafts of mouse glioma and human GBM cells, and living, passage-zero GBM patient tumor tissues tested ex vivo on an organotypic brain slice culture (OBSC)-based platform (23). Here, building on these proof-of-concept studies, we investigated the effects of TMZ+EdU treatment for GBM, reasoning that their distinct mechanisms of action and the conceptual improbability of resistance to EdU-given its close structural similarity to thymidine-might reduce recurrence rates and even enable durable remission in a subset of patients. To this end, in this study, we tested the synergistic effect of TMZ+EdU in three different GBM cell lines in vitro, in in vivo orthotopic mouse models of GBM, and in living, passage-zero GBM patient tumor tissues seeded on OBSCs. Our results show the combination of TMZ and EdU yield synergistic effects against GBM. 2 of 11 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2532187123 pnas.org

div.head: Targeted Localization and Pharmacokinetic Features of EdU
div.p: In Vivo. In our previous study, we showed the targeted localization of EdU into the human GBM cell lines seeded on OBSCs (23). In this study, we began by testing the targeted localization of EdU into tumor cells in vivo. We first established orthotopic GBM tumors in female athymic nude mice by inoculating FLuc expressing U87 human GBM cells into their brain parenchyma. Since U87 tumor cells form large and well-demarcated tumors upon intracranial inoculation, we chose this in vivo orthotopic mouse model of GBM to test the targeted localization of EdU into tumor cells in the brain (24,25). Upon confirming tumor establishment via bioluminescence imaging (BLI), we randomized these mice into four different groups to be injected with PBS Control, 200 mg/ kg EdU, 5 mg/kg TMZ, or 5 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/kg EdU. ese injections were administered for 3 consecutive days, and the brains of mice were harvested the following day (~18 h after the last injection) to perform hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), nuclear (DAPI), and EdU staining. In Fig. 2, the tumor mass is seen with H&E staining. Once the tumor cells were confirmed with H&E, EdU staining via click chemistry and nuclear staining (DAPI) was performed on the slices from the same area of the brains. In negative controls, there was no EdU signal detected in either tumor or nontumor cells in the brains of mice administered with PBS or 5 mg/kg TMZ, pointing out the specificity of EdU staining via click chemistry (Fig. 2 A, B, E, and F). On the other hand, the EdU signal (green) was highly localized to the tumor cells in mice treated with both 200 mg/kg EdU (Fig. 2C) and 5 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/kg EdU (Fig. 2D). Quantification of EdU-positive cells in tumor versus nontumor cells revealed ~83 times more EdUpositive cells in 200 mg/kg EdU-treated group and ~70 times more EdU-positive cells in 5 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/kg EdUtreated group (****P < 0.0001 for both comparisons, Fig. 2G).

e residual EdU signal observed in Fig. 2 C and D was localized mostly to the subventricular zone (SVZ) of the brain, which is known to harbor some proliferative cells (26). ese results confirmed the highly targeted localization of EdU into tumor cells in vivo. To our knowledge, EdU's distribution in plasma and brain has not been characterized. To characterize this biodistribution and clearance of EdU in vivo, we performed a pharmacokinetic study with healthy female athymic nude mice. We administered a single dose of 200 mg/kg EdU, collected plasma and brain samples from mice at six different time points, and obtained EdU concentrations via LC-MS/MS (Fig. 3A). e maximum plasma concentration of EdU was reached at 15 min at ~73 μg/mL, with a half-life of ~10 min (Fig. 3B and SI Appendix, Fig. S1A). On the other hand, in the brain, the maximum concentration of EdU was reached at 15 min at ~4.8 μg/mL, with a half-life of ~30 min (Fig. 3C and SI Appendix, Fig. S1B). e mean AUC 0-∞ values for plasma and brain were 42.14 and 4.92 μg h/mL (SI Appendix, Fig. S1 A and B), respectively, corresponding to a brain-to-plasma (B/P) AUC ratio of approximately 0.12 for EdU. Together, these results support our hypothesis that EdU localizes into the tumor cells in the brain in vivo.

div.head: Testing TMZ+EdU Combination Therapy In Vitro in Human GBM
div.p: Cells and In Vivo in Orthotopic Mouse Models of GBM. It has been found that combinations of various mutations in oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes give rise to GBM (27). Human GBM cell lines derived from patients are widely used in testing drug candidates both in vitro and in vivo. To recapitulate this heterogeneous genetic profile, in our study, we used three human GBM cell lines with different sets of mutations (25,(28)(29)(30)(31)(32)(33) in testing the combination of TMZ and EdU: U87, GBM8, and LN229. All of these cell lines are engineered to express firefly luciferase (FLuc), and thus, bioluminescence signal measured upon incubation with luciferin is used as a measure of viability. We tested these cell lines with the standard-of-care drug TMZ, EdU, and the TMZ+EdU combination. Testing was done by cell survival assay in vitro and by monitoring survival and tumor growth in vivo in female athymic nude mice bearing orthotopic xenografts of these 3 cell lines.

div.head: Testing TMZ+EdU Combination Therapy In Vitro in the U87 Cell
div.p: Line and in Mice Bearing Orthotopic Xenografts of U87. We first tested for potential synergistic effects of TMZ and EdU in U87 cells in vitro. We have reported the IC50 value of EdU for this cell line as 40 μM (23). Cell survival with the combination of EdU at this concentration and various doses of TMZ showed that these two drugs are synergistic, especially at the higher doses of TMZ (SI Appendix, Fig. S2A). is in vitro synergism between TMZ and EdU encouraged us to test this combination in vivo in the mice bearing orthotopic xenografts of U87 cells. To establish the orthotopic mouse model with the U87 cell line, we inoculated U87 cells intracranially into the brain parenchyma of female athymic nude mice and confirmed establishment of tumors via BLI. Informed by our pharmacokinetic results with EdU, we administered EdU at 200 mg/kg every Monday-Friday (M-F), once per day, and TMZ at 5 mg/kg every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday (MWF) for a total of 6 wk (Fig. 3 B and C and SI Appendix, Fig. S1 A and B). For the combination group, mice received the TMZ injections in the morning and EdU injections in the afternoon with the indicated regimens for 6 wk. Upon randomization of mice into PBS control and three treatment groups on Day 7 (SI Appendix, Fig. S2B), we monitored the tumor growth of these mice via BLI. Neither 200 mg/kg EdU nor 5 mg/kg TMZ treatment showed a successful suppression of tumor growth while the treatment with the combination of 200 mg/kg EdU and 5 mg/kg TMZ suppressed the tumor growth and decreased the tumor signal below the baseline level (Fig. 4A). is suppression lasted as long as the injections continued. However, once the injections were completed by Day 46, the tumors recurred in 7 to 10 d, and the mice started to reach humane endpoint after ~15 d following discontinuation of the treatment (Fig. 4A). Fig. 4B shows the BLI images of representative mice throughout the study (see SI Appendix, Fig. S2 B-G for extended BLI images). While treatment with single-agent 200 mg/kg EdU and 5 mg/ kg TMZ extended the survival by ~30% and ~50%, respectively, compared to the PBS control group (P < 0.0008 and P < 0.0001, respectively), combination of 5 mg/kg TMZ and 200 mg/kg EdU extended the survival by more than 130% compared to the PBS control group (P < 0.0001). Additionally, the combination group extended the survival by ~60% and ~80% compared to the single-agent TMZ and EdU groups, respectively (P < 0.0001 for both comparisons, Fig. 4C). At the study endpoint, 1 out of 8 mice in the combination group was alive and showed no detectable tumor BLI signal or detectable tumor cells at or around the tumor cell inoculation site, resulting in ~12% survival in 5 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/kg EdU group (Fig. 4C and SI Appendix, Fig. S2 G and H). us, we concluded that TMZ and EdU combination showed a synergistic effect in vivo in suppressing the tumor growth and increased the survival in mice bearing orthotopic xenografts of U87 cells.

div.head: Testing the Synergistic Effect of TMZ and EdU Combination In Vitro in the GBM8 Cell Line and in Mice Bearing Orthotopic
div.p: Xenografts of GBM8. We next tested the potential synergy of TMZ and EdU in the GBM8 cell line in vitro. Previously, the IC50 value of EdU for this cell line was identified as ~50 nM (23). Cell survival assay combining this IC50 value of EdU with various doses of TMZ showed synergistic to additive effect at high TMZ doses (SI Appendix, Fig. S3A). us, the synergism observed in GBM8 was not as high as that in U87 in the cell survival assay.

We next established the orthotopic mouse model by inoculating GBM8 cells intracranially into the brain parenchyma of female athymic nude mice. After confirmation of tumor establishment via BLI, mice were randomized into PBS control and treatment groups on Day 9 (SI Appendix, Fig. S3B). Considering the inherent sensitivity of GBM8 cell line to TMZ, we chose two different TMZ doses in this model; low dose (1 mg/kg) and high dose (5 mg/kg). For EdU treatment, we used 200 mg/kg again as in the U87 in vivo model, considering the fast clearance of the molecule (Fig. 3 B and C and SI Appendix, Fig. S1 A and B). e combination groups featured combination of 1 mg/kg TMZ and 200 mg/kg EdU and the combination of 5 mg/kg TMZ and 200 mg/ kg EdU, separately. As in the U87 in vivo model, 6 wk of injections were administered with the M-F and MWF treatment regimens for EdU and TMZ, respectively. Unlike the U87 in vivo model, following the end of 6 wk of injections, we wanted to investigate tumor recurrence and response to maintenance therapy in all treatment groups. us, we set a recurrence criteria per mouse where treatment was resumed when the tumor's BLI signal increased to ≥10× its baseline (initial) value and a discontinuation criteria per mouse where reinjections were discontinued once the tumor's BLI signal returned to and stabilized at the baseline level.

e tumor growth was assessed via BLI in two phases: first phase during the administration of 6 wk of injections (Day 7 to Day 50) and the second phase during the monitoring of tumor recurrence and response to as-needed maintenance therapy (Day 50 to study endpoint, Day 170).

div.head: Assessment of Tumor Growth and Recurrence during the First
Phase of Treatment and the Second Phase of Maintenance
div.p: Therapy in Mice Bearing Orthotopic Xenografts of GBM8. During the first phase, we observed suppression of tumor growth in all mice except those that received PBS and 1 mg/kg TMZ (Fig. 5 A and C and SI Appendix, Figs. S3 B and C and S4 A and C). During the second phase, when the initial treatment regimen had been discontinued, we started to observe recurrence in some mice in the 5 mg/kg TMZ, 200 mg/kg EdU, and 1 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/ kg EdU groups and initiated maintenance therapy on recurrent mice on Days 59 and 63 (Fig. 5 B and C and SI Appendix, Fig. S4 B, D, and E). Recurrence occurred in ~60% (4 out of 7) of mice in the 5 mg/kg TMZ group, 100% (6 out of 6) of mice in the 200 mg/kg EdU group, and ~15% (1 out of 7) of mice in the 1 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/kg EdU group (SI Appendix, Fig. S4 B, D, and E; see SI Appendix, Fig. S3 D-G for extended BLI images). In contrast, no recurrence was observed in any mice in the 5 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/kg EdU group (Fig. 5 B and C and SI Appendix, Fig. S4F). According to the tumors' BLI signals, none of the recurred mice in the 5 mg/kg TMZ group responded to maintenance therapy while 50% of the recurred mice in the 200 mg/kg EdU group responded to maintenance therapy and showed remission (Fig. 5B and SI Appendix, Fig. S4 B and E). One case of recurrence observed in the 1 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/kg EdU group also showed suppression of tumor growth and eventually remission upon receiving maintenance therapy (Fig. 5 B and C and SI Appendix, Figs. S3 D-G and S4D). From these results, we concluded that maintenance therapy with single-agent EdU and combination of TMZ and EdU helped with suppressing the tumor growth while maintenance therapy with single-agent TMZ did not provide any benefit in suppressing the tumor growth.

Monitoring Survival in Mice Bearing Orthotopic Xenografts of GBM8. In addition to assessing tumor growth and recurrence, we monitored survival throughout the study in the in vivo GBM8 model. At the study endpoint, single-agent treatments with 1 mg/kg TMZ, 5 mg/kg TMZ, and 200 mg/kg EdU extended the survival significantly by ~10%, ~200%, and ~260%, respectively, compared to the PBS control group (P = 0.0037, P = 0.0005, and P = 0.0011, respectively, Fig. 5D). Moreover, 50% of mice (3 out of 6 mice) in 200 mg/kg EdU group and ~30% of mice (2 out of 7 mice) in 5 mg/kg TMZ group were alive by the study endpoint. Importantly, all of the mice in 1 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/kg EdU and 5 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/kg combination groups were alive and tumor-free by the study endpoint, conferring a complete survival at the study endpoint in this stringent patientderived model and highlighting the strong therapeutic potential of TMZ+EdU combination (Fig. 5D). We concluded from these results that the combination of TMZ and EdU conferred a synergistic effect in terms of both suppressing the tumor growth and extending the survival in mice bearing orthotopic xenografts of GBM8 cells. Combined with the results of the U87 in vivo model, these results supported our hypothesis that combining TMZ and EdU could yield a greater therapeutic effect than either of these drugs confers alone.

div.head: Testing TMZ+EdU Combination Therapy In Vitro in the LN229 Cell
div.p: Line and in Mice Bearing Orthotopic Xenografts of LN229. Upon observing these synergistic results with the GBM8 in vivo model, we wished to test this synergistic effect in a third orthotopic in vivo model using LN229 cell line. We first assayed cell survival to test the synergistic effect of TMZ+EdU in vitro by combining the IC50 value of EdU for LN229 [~20 μM, as identified previously (23)] with various doses of TMZ. As in the other two GBM cell lines, the TMZ+EdU combination was more efficient than either drug alone at higher concentrations of TMZ (SI Appendix,

We then created the in vivo orthotopic model by inoculating LN229 cells intracranially into the brain parenchyma of female athymic nude mice. Upon confirming the establishment of tumors via BLI, we stratified the mice into PBS control and five treatment groups on Day 4 (SI Appendix, Fig. S5B). We chose the same treatment groups and treatment regimen with 6 wk of injections as in the GBM8 in vivo model. By the third week of injections, mice in the PBS control group started to reach humane endpoint while the tumors' BLI signals in all the other groups, except 200 mg/kg EdU group, decreased below the baseline level, indicating suppression of tumor growth (Fig. 6 A and B and SI Appendix, Fig. S5C). On the other hand, 200 mg/kg EdU treatment was only able to stabilize the tumors' BLI signals at ~3 times the baseline level signal. By the completion of 6 wk of injections on Day 46, all the mice in the PBS control group reached humane endpoint and the tumors' BLI signals in 200 mg/kg EdU groups started to increase (Fig. 6A). However, the tumors' BLI signals in TMZ single-agent and TMZ+EdU combination groups decreased further and stabilized ~0.01 times the baseline levels (Fig. 6A and SI Appendix, Fig. S5D). Around a month after the completion of injections by Day 70, mice treated with 200 mg/kg EdU started to reach humane endpoint while tumors' BLI signals in combination or single-agent TMZ groups remained lower than the baseline level signal (Fig. 6A and SI Appendix, Fig. S5E ). Additionally, around Day 80 in 25% (2 out of 8 mice) of mice in 1 m/kg TMZ group and around Day 85 in ~12% (1 out of 8 mice) of mice in 5 mg/kg TMZ group, we started to observe some recurrence (Fig. 6 A and B and SI Appendix, Fig. S5 F and G ). However, this recurrence was not observed in either of the combination groups. For survival, treatment with 200 mg/kg EdU extended the median survival significantly by ~110% compared to the PBS control group (P = 0.0002, Fig. 6C). At conclusion of the study, none of the mice in 5 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/kg EdU group reached the humane endpoint, resulting in a striking and significant increase in median survival compared to both PBS control and single-agent EdU treatment groups (P < 0.0001 and P = 0.0008, respectively, Fig. 6C). Similarly, 1 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/kg EdU group extended the survival significantly compared to both PBS control and single-agent EdU group (P < 0.0001 and P = 0.0018, respectively, Fig. 6C). In 1 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/ kg EdU group, only one mouse reached humane endpoint due to orbital infection, although its tumor had much lower BLI signal compared to the baseline level, corresponding to ~88% survival at the study endpoint. However, different from our results in U87 GBM8 in vivo models, in the LN229 in vivo model, we observed that combination of TMZ and EdU performed as well the single-agent TMZ groups, leading to an additive effect in suppressing the tumor growth and prolonging the median survival (Fig. 6C and SI Appendix, Fig. S5 F and G). Collectively, the results from our in vivo orthotopic mouse models of GBM established with U87, GBM8, and LN229 cells provided preclinical evidence that TMZ+EdU combination could elicit a synergistic to partly additive effect in GBM.

div.head: Toxicity Profiling of Mice Treated with EdU, TMZ, and Their Combination in In Vivo Orthotopic Mouse Model of U87 and GBM8.
div.p: To identify treatment-related toxicity, we collected peripheral organs (small intestine, kidney, spleen, liver, and lung) from mice bearing orthotopic U87 or GBM8 xenografts treated with PBS, EdU, TMZ, or TMZ+EdU combination for microscopic evaluation. Tissues were fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin, routinely processed to paraffin, sectioned to 5 µm, H&E-stained, and evaluated by a board-certified veterinary pathologist (SI Appendix, Fig. S6 A and B). EdU-(with or without TMZ) related findings were identified in both U87 and GBM8 engrafted animals in the small intestine and spleen compared to PBS-treated control animals. Treatmentrelated findings were not identified with TMZ.
Increased small intestinal crypt epithelial necrosis/apoptosis (minimal to mild) was identified in the small intestine of animals which were being dosed with EdU or TMZ+EdU at time of killing.

is was associated with minimal to mild increases in crypt epithelial mitotic figures compared to PBS-treated control animals, which likely reflects a regenerative response to epithelial cell injury. In the small intestine of mice in which treatment with EdU or TMZ+EdU had been discontinued prior to necropsy, there were either no findings or increased crypt epithelial mitotic figures as compared to PBS-treated animals, suggestive of recovery from previous crypt injury. Increased extramedullary hematopoiesis was identified in the spleen of mice which were being dosed with EdU alone or in combination with TMZ at the time of necropsy. is is interpreted to reflect a regenerative hematopoietic response (common in rodents) to presumed bone marrow toxicity (no hematology or bone marrow histology from these animals available to confirm). Findings identified in other tissues were interpreted as incidental age-related or common background findings that were not test article-related. No toxicity was identified in the liver or kidneys after treatment with EdU, TMZ, or TMZ+EdU combinations. Overall, across both models, EdU, alone or with TMZ, had minimal to mild and reversible test article-related effects in the small intestine (primary) and spleen (secondary), consistent with injury to rapidly dividing cells. e reversibility of these mild effects is also supported by the recovery of body weight after treatment in mice bearing U87, GBM8, and LN229 tumors (SI Appendix, Fig. S7 A -C ).

We also wanted to test the effect of treatments on complete blood counts. To this end, we collected blood samples from mice bearing LN229 tumors on three different days: two of them during the 6 wk of injections (Day 16 and Day 30) and one after the completion of 6 wk of injections (Day 58). Complete blood count showed there were only minor and reversible differences between the counts of White Blood Cells (WBCs), Lymphocytes (LYMPH), Neutrophils (NEUT), Basophils (BASO), Eosinophils (EO), and Red Blood Cells (RBC) values in PBS control group on Day 16 and in all the other groups (SI Appendix, Fig. S8 A -F ). Additionally, the mild decrease observed in RBC counts on Day 30 during the treatment in EdU-and TMZ+EdU-treated mice overlaps with the inferred bone marrow toxicity from histopathological evaluation of U87 and GBM8-bearing mice (SI Appendix, Fig. S8F ). However, for all the counts of these different cells, the values in all groups were mainly at or above the normal lower limit values after the dosing ended by Day 58 (SI Appendix, Fig. S8 A -F). ese results, together with the results on the histopathological and body weight changes, further confirmed that EdU, alone or in combination with TMZ, induced mild, transient, and reversible toxicity.

Testing TMZ+EdU Combination Therapy against Living, Passage-Zero GBM Patient Tumor Tissues Ex Vivo. Upon collecting these promising results, we proceeded to test the efficacy of TMZ+EdU on living, passage-zero GBM patient tumor tissues seeded atop OBSCs (23,34,35). In our previous investigation of EdU as a potential therapeutic for GBM, we observed differential response across all patient tumors tested with monotherapy EdU or TMZ (23). In these new experiments, we observed a similar trend. We exposed four IDH-wild-type WHO-classified passage-zero GBM patient tumor tissues to single-agent EdU or TMZ as well as a combination of both compounds. 3 out of 4 of these tissue samples (PT1, PT3, and PT4) were from patients who clinically showed rapid tumor progression after receiving TMZ.

During treatment, TMZ and/or EdU were added under the transwell membranes supporting each tumor-bearing OBSC and allowed to diffuse through the OBSCs and into the tumor cells. All tumors were treated with EdU and/or TMZ at doses of 0, 100, 250, and 1,000 µM. Combination therapy of [TMZ + EdU] was given at doses of [0, 0], [100, 100], [250, 250] and [1,000 µM, 1,000 µM]. Among the tissues tested, we observed several doses where EdU alone or in combination with TMZ performed better than TMZ alone (Fig. 7 A -D). Using the Zero Interaction Potency (ZIP) Synergy score (36 , 37) that measures the difference between observed effects of a combinatorial regimen and expected effects if individual drugs are not interactive, we found that the effect of the combinatorial therapy ranged from additive (0 < ZIP < 10 in PT2, PT3, PT4) to synergistic (ZIP > 10 in PT1) (Fig. 7E ).

GBM tumors have significant intra-and intertumoral heterogeneity; therapies that are effective for some patients may not be effective for others, and vice versa. We therefore tested EdU against two passage-zero GBM patient tumor tissues in combination with a range of other FDA-approved chemotherapies. We chose carboplatin and lomustine because of their cell cycle-independent antitumor activity to complement EdU's hypothesized activity during the S-phase (38 , 39), and also because lomustine is frequently used as a control arm in trials and sometimes considered the standard of care after GBM progression (38 , 40). We chose etoposide because its mechanism of action through the stabilization of the topoisomerase II-DNA cleavage complex is very different from EdU's and may elicit different downstream compensatory mechanisms. It has also been well tolerated in heavily pretreated patients with refractory gliomas (41 , 42). We also chose the poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase-1 inhibitor (PARPi) Olaparib because it is under investigation as a radio and chemosensitizer (43 , 44). As such, it might potentiate EdU's ability to target glioma stem cells (GSCs) which have upregulated PARP that promotes base excision repair and the repair of single-strand breaks in treated cancer cells (45 ).

To assess these exploratory combinatorial regimens, we first used doses previously determined to be near the ED50 values of each single agent. We then combined these drugs with 1,000 µM EdU. Across all drugs tested in combination, we observed more killing in the combination groups than when the drug was used alone (Fig. 7 F and G). Notably, at the same doses, each patient tissue responded differently to each drug. For instance, in PT4, there was a 2.9-fold increase in tumor killing when EdU was added to etoposide, but just a 1.2-fold increase in PT1, (Fig. 7 F and G), further highlighting the need for more personalized and patient-centric models that capture patient-to-patient heterogeneity.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: As the most common primary malignancy of the central nervous system, GBM carries an extremely poor prognosis, with only ~7% of patients surviving five years after diagnosis (46 -48 ). erefore, pnas.org there is a need for improved GBM treatments. Current efforts focus on investigating the therapeutic potential of different drugs combined with TMZ, the first-line chemotherapeutic for GBM. However, despite trials and preclinical studies with agents such as lomustine (49), bevacizumab (50), and PARP inhibitors (51 , 52 ), none of these combinations have received FDA approval to date.

Here, we demonstrated in i) GBM cell lines in vitro, ii) orthotopic mouse models of GBM in vivo, and iii) living, passage-zero GBM patient tumor tissues on OBSC that EdU shows a synergistic effect in GBM when combined with TMZ. Moreover, we characterized the pharmacokinetic features of EdU and confirmed the targeted localization of EdU into GBM tumor cells in vivo in both single-agent EdU-treated and combination-treated mice.

Our results on pharmacokinetic characteristics of EdU in vivo highlighted the fast clearance of EdU with limited penetrance to the blood-brain barrier and suggested that there is room for improvement to modulate the bioavailability of EdU via formulation. Formulating EdU would increase the bioavailability and in turn the penetrance of EdU to blood-brain barrier, potentiating the effect observed in combination with TMZ.

In our U87 in vivo model, we observed only a partial increase in survival with single-agent TMZ and EdU while neither was able to suppress the tumor growth. However, combination of TMZ and EdU showed a truly synergistic effect in this model by both suppressing the tumor growth and extending the survival drastically. On the other hand, in our GBM8 in vivo model, single-agent EdU and TMZ (5 mg/kg) treatments conferred considerable survival benefit compared to the PBS control group. Nevertheless, we also observed recurrence in these single-agent treatment groups with partial to no response to maintenance therapy. For instance, we observed recurrence and no response to maintenance therapy in ~60% of the mice treated with 5 mg/kg TMZ, reflecting the acquired resistance following an initial positive response to TMZ treatment. Notably, this TMZ resistance was overcome in mice treated with 5 mg/kg TMZ + 200 mg/kg EdU since no recurrence was observed in these mice by the study endpoint. ese results point out the power of TMZ+EdU combination in targeting the TMZ-resistant tumors which is a prevalent occurrence in the clinic.

Surprisingly, in our third in vivo model with LN229, we observed that single-agent TMZ treatments initially performed as well as the combination treatment groups, indicating an additive effect in this model. However, both single-agent TMZ groups exhibited recurrence following the completion of 6 wk of injections. Combination groups in this LN229 model, on the other hand, avoided this recurrence, similar to the results in the GBM8 model while the survival benefit these combination treatments conferred compared to the single-agent treatments was not as drastic as in the GBM8 model. e difference among these different in vivo models of GBM could be attributed to the heterogeneous nature of this disease and the differences among the genetic alterations harbored by these GBM cell lines. Further in vivo studies in these and other models featuring various doses of EdU in combination with TMZ could identify lower doses of EdU that still show synergistic effect.

Furthermore, on our OBSC platform, TMZ+EdU acted in an additive or synergistic manner against all four passage-zero GBM patient tumor tissues. e more muted responses reflect what one may expect to observe in the clinical setting, where tumors with heterogeneity in proliferation rate and mutational drivers are typically not responsive to TMZ alone and respond incrementally to combination therapies. e heterogeneity of patient-to-patient response also highlights the need for more personalized and patient-centric models in drug development. Our OBSC platform may therefore serve as a functional correlative biomarker to identify patients most likely to benefit from TMZ+EdU or other combinatorial regimens. Expanding OBSC testing of EdU to a larger, molecularly diverse cohort could refine the estimated prevalence of synergy, enable biomarker discovery, and further advance functional precision medicine efforts in GBM.

div.head: New Therapeutic Avenues to Pursue: EdU's Potential in
div.p: Combination with Various Other Chemotherapeutics. Our results on combining EdU with various other chemotherapeutics against GBM patient tumor tissues revealed the transformative role EdU could play in alternative treatment regimens for GBM. By targeting complementary mechanisms of action in these combinations, we found patient-specific sensitivities to different combination therapies. Future studies of the mechanism and therapeutic potential of these combinatorial regimens will shed light on the clinical utility of each in GBM. Such personalized combination regimens in GBM treatment could provide muchneeded alternative therapies.

div.head: Materials and Methods
div.p: Cell Lines. U87 (purchased from ATCC in 2012, catalog #: HTB-14, RRID: CVCL_0022) and LN229 (purchased from ATCC in 2012, catalog #: CRL-2611, RRID: CVCL_0393) cells were cultured in 1× DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin. Patient-derived GBM8 cells (a kind gift from H. Wakimoto, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA) (28,29) were cultured in neurobasal-A medium (Gibco, catalog #: 12349015) supplemented with 1 mg heparin (STEMCELL Technologies, catalog #: 07980), 10 μg FGF (Shenandoah Biotechnology, catalog #: 100-146), 10 mL B27 supplement (Life Technologies Inc., catalog #: A3582801), 7.5 mL L-glutamine (Life Technologies Inc., catalog #: 10888022), 10 μg EGF (Shenandoah Biotechnology, catalog #: 100-26-100 μg), 2.5 mL N2 supplement (Life Technologies Inc., catalog #: 17502048), and 2.5 mL Antibiotic-Antimycotic (100×) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, catalog #: 15240062).

div.head: Lentiviral Vectors (LVs).
div.p: The following LV was used in this study: mCherry protein fused to firefly luciferase (LV-mCh-FL). This LV also encodes a puromycin resistance gene. U87, GBM8, and LN229 cell lines were transduced with this LV-mCh-FL. Following transduction, mCherry expression was confirmed, and cells expressing mCherry were selected using puromycin treatment.

TMZ, EdU, and various drugs were administered to cultured cells in vitro, and to models of human GBM including xenograft mouse models and patient tissue samples seeded on OBSCs. Consequently, we measured survival, tumor response, markers in tissue sections and blood, PK, and tissue drug concentrations. Details of experimental designs, procedures, and analyses are provided in SI Appendix, Supplemental Methods.

Data, Materials, and Software Availability. All study data are included in the article and/or SI Appendix. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS. We also acknowledge University of North Carolina Biomedical Research Imaging Center, University of North Carolina Advanced Translational Pharmacology and Analytical Chemistry Core, University of North Carolina Animal Clinical Chemistry Core, and University of North Carolina Screening Live Cancer Explants Core.
